What Makes Customers Recommend a Clothing Product?

Predicting recommendation likelihood from review sentiment, ratings, age, and department using statistical and ML methods.

01 Motivation

E-commerce platforms live and die by their recommendation systems. Understanding what drives a customer to actively recommend a clothing product — beyond just leaving a high rating — is valuable for both sellers and platform designers. A customer who recommends a product is more likely to return and to influence others.

This project asks: can we predict whether a customer will recommend a clothing item based on their age, their rating, the sentiment of their review, and the product department? The answer has direct implications for targeted marketing and product quality feedback loops.

🎯 Research Question

Can we predict customer recommendation status from demographic and review-based features?

💡 Why It Matters

Recommendation prediction enables proactive customer engagement — identifying at-risk customers before they churn, and identifying brand advocates to reward.

02 Data Source

The dataset is the Women's Clothing E-Commerce Reviews dataset from Kaggle, containing 22,628 reviews across multiple departments and age groups. The data was enriched with two derived features: Review Length (word count) and Sentiment Polarity (computed via TextBlob).

FeatureTypeDescription
AgeNumericReviewer age
RatingNumeric (1–5)Star rating given to the product
Recommended INDBinary target1 = recommends, 0 = does not
Positive Feedback CountNumericHelpfulness votes from other users
Department / Division NameCategoricalProduct category
Review LengthEngineeredWord count of the written review
SentimentEngineeredTextBlob polarity score (−1 to +1)

Class imbalance note: ~82% of reviews are positive recommendations. This was accounted for by using F1 score (not accuracy) as the primary evaluation metric and using stratified train/test splits.

04 Hypothesis Testing

Four hypothesis tests were conducted at α = 0.05.

TestMethodp-valueDecision
HT1: Age differs between recommenders and non-recommenders Two-sample t-test < 0.001 Reject H₀
HT2: Recommenders write more positive reviews (sentiment) Welch's t-test (one-tailed) < 0.001 Reject H₀
HT3: Mean rating differs across departments One-Way ANOVA < 0.001 Reject H₀
HT4: Review length differs by recommendation status Welch's t-test (two-tailed) < 0.001 Reject H₀

Interpretation: All four tests rejected H₀, confirming that age, sentiment, department, and review length all have statistically significant relationships with recommendation status. This gives a strong statistical foundation for the ML models.

HT2 — Sentiment KDE: recommenders are clearly more positive.
HT3 — Rating by department: Trend department scores lowest.

05 Machine Learning

Classification target: Recommended IND. Features: 12 total (5 numeric + 7 one-hot encoded). Train: 18,102 samples / Test: 4,526 samples. Stratified split to preserve class imbalance.

Model comparison — all three classifiers perform strongly above 92%.
Logistic Regression ROC curve — AUC = 0.969.

Note on high accuracy: The strong performance (92–93%) is largely driven by Rating, which is highly correlated with recommendation status (r ≈ 0.79). The Decision Tree achieves its best split at depth=1, meaning a single feature threshold separates most of the data.

K-Means Clustering (k=4) — Customer Segments

Four customer segments identified: young enthusiasts (high sentiment, high rec rate), critical middle-aged shoppers (low rating, low rec rate), older satisfied customers (high age, high rating), and brief positive reviewers (short reviews, very high sentiment).

PCA — Dimensionality Reduction

9 components needed for 90% explained variance. 2-D projection shows clear separation between recommended and not-recommended classes.

06 Key Findings

⭐

Rating is the strongest predictor. Rating correlates with recommendation at r ≈ 0.79. A single decision tree split on Rating achieves 93% accuracy, confirming it dominates all other features.

💬

Sentiment matters significantly. HT2 confirmed that recommenders write far more positive reviews (mean sentiment 0.277 vs 0.129). This is the second most important feature after Rating.

👩

Older customers are slightly more likely to recommend. HT1 found a statistically significant age difference (mean 43.5 vs 42.4), though the effect size is small.

👗

Department affects ratings. The Trend department scores significantly lower (mean 3.84) vs Intimate (4.28), suggesting product-category quality varies meaningfully.

🤖

All three classifiers perform above 92%, with the Decision Tree edging out at F1=0.958. The high performance underlines that recommendation prediction is tractable with basic features.

🗂️

K-Means reveals four natural customer archetypes — from brief-but-positive reviewers to detailed critical shoppers — which could inform personalized engagement strategies.

07 Limitations & Future Work

⚠️ Limitations

Rating dominance. Rating is so strongly correlated with recommendation that models may not truly generalise — they mostly learn "high rating = recommend."

Class imbalance. 82% positive rate means even a naive classifier scores 82%. F1 mitigates this but future work should explore oversampling (SMOTE).

No product features. Clothing attributes (size, colour, material) were not available, limiting the model's ability to capture product-level effects.

🚀 Future Work

Deep NLP on review text. BERT or fine-tuned transformers on the full review text could capture nuanced reasoning behind recommendations.

Remove Rating as a feature to test whether the model can predict recommendation from softer signals alone — a harder but more interesting problem.

Product-level features. Incorporating product metadata (price, material, fit feedback) would add a richer predictive dimension.
